## 1. What was read

**906 research articles** from 32 of the 33 journals on the roster.

A further **207** records (19% of the 1,113 this month's harvest returned) carry no abstract and are not research: news, correspondence, editor highlights and obituaries. PubMed types them `Journal Article` and nothing else, so the publication-type filter cannot see them — across the whole index they are 22.7% of it and 35% of `general`, and 3,801 of them are JAMA. Every count below is over the full harvest and is inflated by this; the figure above is not.

| General | Cancer | Immune | Bioinfo | Sysbio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 407 | 189 | 83 | 413 | 21 |

!!! warning "Volume swing against the median month: bioinfo +52%"
    Check the source before reading anything into this. Two benign causes account for most of these. `bioinfo` every January carries the Nucleic Acids Research database issue and runs high. And several journals simply deposit nothing in some months: across the 44 months read, 4 of 33 journals are absent from at least one, worst being *Nat Mach Intell* (20 months missing, 81 papers in total) and *Bioinformatics* (4 months missing, 2,905 papers in total). This month is missing *Genome Res*. Queried directly, PubMed returns zero for those journal-months too — the holes are in the source, reproduced exactly by re-running the harvest. So a swing here is not evidence that a field went quiet, and is not usually evidence that the pipeline broke either.

Largest contributors: Nucleic Acids Res 255, Nature 85, JAMA 79, Science 77, Bioinformatics 48, Lancet 41.

## 3. The evidence that moved it







!!! note "Written 2026-08-26, in arrears"
    2024 was added to the corpus nineteen months after the practice started,
    to test whether its "first appearance" claims survived a lower floor. None
    of them did. These twelve briefings are therefore written backwards, by
    someone who already knows what 2025 and 2026 did, and that is the opposite
    of the position the monthly practice is supposed to simulate. Read them as
    a baseline for the threads, not as a record of what was visible at the time.
    2024 was also read thread-first rather than exhaustively, so its card counts
    are a floor and are **not** comparable with 2025 and 2026 month totals.

**The agent era starts here, thirteen months before this corpus said it did.**
[38799228](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38799228/) (*Nat Mach Intell*) gives a large language model chemistry tools
and has it plan and execute syntheses. Until today the corpus dated the first
LLM-agent paper to ESCARGOT on 4 February 2025 and built a diffusion-lag
argument on it. That argument is void. The tool-using agent is in a tracked
journal in January 2024, and [38341654](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38341654/) (GeneGPT) follows in February.

**AlphaFold's own limits, stated in its own field's methods journal.**
[38036854](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38036854/) (*Nat Methods*): AlphaFold predictions are valuable hypotheses
that accelerate but **do not replace** experimental structure determination.
The most successful predictive model in biology publishes its own ceiling in
January 2024.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    This paragraph continued: "Alongside it, [38082179](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38082179/) reports that
    macroscopic resting-state brain dynamics are best described by *linear*
    models — a simple-beats-complex title in the same month. The corpus
    previously dated that genre to mid-2025." The paper is real and its result is
    as stated: linear autoregressive models fit intracranial EEG and fMRI better
    than nonlinear families across 822 participants on predictive power,
    complexity and unexplained residual dynamics, and it names four reasons
    microscopic nonlinearity is masked at the macroscopic scale. It has nothing
    to do with foundation models — no pretraining, no scale, no transfer — and
    was put on that thread because "simple beats complex" is a phrase the thread
    uses. That is an analogy between two titles, not evidence, and the card no
    longer carries `foundation-models`. It stays on `method-credibility`, where
    the abstract does state a standing assumption and challenge it.

**Two neural-immune mechanisms, in the two highest-tier venues.**
[38134932](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38134932/) (*Cell*): sensory neurons promote immune homeostasis in the
lung. [38085267](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38085267/) adds commensal bacteria driving type I
interferon to maintain tolerance. Between them the thread this corpus scores as
its healthiest is running on all three of its arms — neural, microbial, lymphoid
— in the first month of the window.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    This paragraph also cited [37947393](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37947393/), "gliomas hijack adaptive
    plasticity to strengthen neuron-tumour synapses", as a third mechanism. It is
    not a mechanism and not a January 2024 result: it is a one-sentence *Cancer
    Discovery* Research Watch item on page 13, with no named authors, whose whole
    abstract is "Blocking BDNF-driven synaptic plasticity extends survival in
    patient-derived glioma xenograft models". It restates [37914930](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37914930/), the
    *Nature* paper this corpus already cards in November 2023 and discusses in
    that month's briefing. One study, two cards, and the thread's opening was
    credited to the echo. The Research Watch card is now `neutral`; the primary
    paper keeps the finding.

## 4. Refutations

### (a) Landing on a tracked thread

[37874957](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37874957/): recent bendamustine before apheresis degrades CAR-T
outcomes — the product's efficacy is contingent on prior therapy in a way the
label did not anticipate. It is the one thread-relevant refutation this month
adds to `cell-therapy` that was not already on the ledger.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    This section opened on [38071995](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38071995/), "the FDA opens an investigation into
    secondary lymphomas after CAR-T", and argued that the platform's safety case
    is reopened by a regulator rather than by a trial. The regulatory action is
    real; the card is not a second instance of it. The record is a single-page
    *Lancet Oncology* news brief on page 21, one staff writer, no abstract,
    reporting the same investigation as [38071978](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38071978/) — the *Lancet* news brief
    one month earlier, already carded and already read as this refutation in the
    December 2023 briefing. Counting the echo let one regulatory action move the
    `cell-therapy` ratio twice, and put it in January when it belongs in
    December. The January card is now `neutral`.

[38296595](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38296595/) (*JITC*): **no** detrimental association between antibiotic use
and checkpoint inhibitor therapy, in a cohort assembled to find one. A widely
repeated microbiome-adjacent clinical claim fails to replicate, and it fails in
the same month the mechanistic microbiome papers above are being published.

### (b) Method credibility

[38150261](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38150261/) (*JAMA*): a large language model reproduces affiliation bias
when reviewing abstracts. The audit of machine judgement begins in the same
months as its adoption, not after it — a pattern that holds for every AI
modality in this corpus once the window is wide enough to see it.

[38172966](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38172966/) benchmarks differential-abundance methods for finding
condition-specific cells across multi-sample single-cell datasets.
